entries.note: This is a recommendation to demand greater scrutiny and timelines.

entries.test: Public technical documentation and intellectual-property disclosures could establish whether advanced AI software companies depend on OpenAI or Anthropic models and possess only the assets described.
entries.note: The universal claim can be challenged by companies developing their own models or owning additional substantive intellectual property.

entries.test: Public financial statements and funding histories could show whether generative AI businesses can operate profitably without continuing venture subsidies.
entries.note: The claim asserts inherent unprofitability and funding dependence despite its introductory hedge.

entries.test: Financial disclosures and fundraising and acquisition activity following the failure of a current AI company would test both funding dependence and the predicted industry-wide financing collapse.
entries.note: The fundraising and acquisition consequences give the otherwise vague death of the narrative a concrete reading.

entries.test: Published token usage, inference prices, operating costs, losses and funding requirements could establish whether increased token consumption produces the asserted chain of higher costs and losses.
entries.note: “Might” qualifies falling unit prices; the cost-and-loss mechanism is asserted firmly.

entries.test: The seven companies’ financial disclosures, unit economics and operating plans could establish their losses and whether any has a financially viable route to profitability.
entries.note: “They” refers to the seven named companies in the preceding sentence.

entries.test: Public fund valuations, venture fundraising and acquisition activity following a named startup’s failure would show whether AI holdings lose at least half their value and investor interest collapses.
entries.note: The passage combines unconditional loss predictions with a startup-failure trigger for the panic.

entries.test: Public financing records, construction schedules and operating results could establish each major institution’s data-center exposure and whether the financed facilities suffer delayed revenue and operating losses.
entries.note: “Take forever” is hyperbole within a concrete claim about financing, delays and losses.
The surrounding sentences supply the timelines and location. Setting Nebius up to fail attributes an intention to Microsoft that impractical deadlines alone cannot establish.

entries.test: Public company financials and financing flows could establish whether generative AI companies lack viable profitability paths and consequently depend on continued external funding.
entries.note: The stress-test metaphor accompanies a concrete assertion about profitability and financing dependence.
He assigns a very small likelihood rather than firmly predicting that most projects will miss those targets.
“Looks far more like” presents a tentative explanation of NVIDIA’s commitments rather than an unqualified finding.
The claim assigns stock manipulation as the exclusive purpose of every GPU expenditure. Public pricing and sales could test the adoption component, but cannot settle that universal motive claim.

entries.test: Public economic data and studies of AI investment’s contribution to output and productivity could establish growth attributable to AI beyond NVIDIA GPU sales and data-center construction.
entries.note: “Driving” attributes economic effects to investment, making this causal. The appearance hedge qualifies an assessment of observable economic results.
